questions.title: Does Louisiana's 'certifying' requirement in La Rev Stat § 9:3550(G)(3)(a) require an original signature on the cancellation notice?
questions.question_body: In Williams v. GoAuto Insurance the Fifth Circuit says that 'certifying' does not necessarily demand a signature and that an electronic statement may satisfy it. Yet earlier Louisiana cases such as Benitez v. Elsayed highlighted the absence of a signed employee identifying who prepared the document as a deficiency. I am unclear whether Louisiana law actually requires any handwritten or original signature on the notice, whether a stamped signature satisfies the requirement, and what authorities support either view.

questions.title: Can an email constitute 'receipt' of a cancellation request under La Rev Stat § 9:3550(G)(3)(b)?
questions.question_body: The opinion holds that GoAuto's computer system receiving an e‑mail from APAC fulfills the statutory 'receipt' requirement even though Black's Law Dictionary defines receipt as taking physical possession. How do Louisiana courts interpret 'receipt' when communications are electronic? Does mere electronic delivery meet the requirement, or must someone physically possess paper copies? Are there controlling decisions interpreting 'receipt' in light of modern technology?

questions.title: How is 'private carrier' defined for delivering insurance-premium-finance cancellation notices under Louisiana law?
questions.question_body: In Williams v. GoAuto the district court treated an APAC employee delivering printed notices as a 'private carrier,' borrowing analogies from Huntley v Bayer MaterialScience about railroads. The Fifth Circuit did not resolve this definition because it accepted email sufficiency instead. What entities qualify as private carriers under La Rev Stat § 9:3550(G)? Specifically, does email transmission count as delivery by a private carrier, or must there be an actual person physically transporting documents?

questions.title: What level of 'strict adherence' does Louisiana require when canceling financed insurance policies—does any minor defect make the cancellation ineffective?
questions.question_body: "Delatte v Lemotte" and "Eaglin v Champion" are cited saying any defect renders a cancellation ineffective, yet Williams v GoAuto allowed GoAuto's automated process despite lacking a pre‑cancellation signature stamp, suggesting some flexibility. How strictly must insurers follow every procedural element listed in La Rev Stat § 9:3550(G)? Does failure to meet even one step automatically invalidate cancellation, or can courts deem minor omissions harmless?

questions.title: When does a federal appellate court certify a state-law question to that state's supreme court, and why did the Fifth Circuit refuse certification in Williams v. GoAuto?
questions.question_body: The panel notes certification should be used sparingly per Jefferson v Lead Indus Ass'n and declines because lack of Supreme Court precedent alone isn't enough. I would like clarification on what criteria trigger certification under 28 U.S.C.§1254(2), how frequently federal courts certify questions from Louisiana courts, and why this particular statutory interpretation issue was deemed inappropriate for certification.

questions.title: What evidentiary burden applies at summary judgment review when parties dispute compliance with a statutory insurance-cancellation procedure?
questions.question_body: Both sides argued over whether GoAuto complied with La Rev Stat § 9:3550(G). The district court granted summary judgment finding compliance based on its own reading of 'receipt' and 'certifying.' I'm unsure how courts allocate proof responsibilities at summary‑judgment stage for strict‑statutory‑compliance disputes—must the moving party prove every element beyond doubt, or can they rely on reasonable doubt raised by the nonmoving party?

questions.title: If an insurer cancels a policy based on an allegedly defective notice under Louisiana law, can insureds still pursue breach-of-good-faith claims?
questions.question_body: The plaintiffs argue that GoAuto's alleged failure to satisfy formalities makes its cancellation ineffective, which could support bad-faith liability even though no valid termination occurred until proper notice is given later. Does an ineffective cancellation automatically give rise to liability for bad faith or breach-of-contract-type duties under Louisiana insurance law, or must insurers first obtain valid termination before such claims arise?

questions.title: How do power-of-attorney provisions in premium-finance agreements allocate responsibility for meeting statutory cancellation requirements between finance company and insurer?
questions.question_body: 'APAC holds power-of-attorney allowing it to cancel policies upon default and must send certified notices to GoAuto per statute.' Yet GoAuto cancels automatically upon receiving APAC's electronic request. Who bears ultimate responsibility—must APAC certify compliance before sending its request while GoAuto merely needs "receipt"—if any step is missing which party is liable for violating La Rev Stat § 9:3550(G)?
